    "description": "Adam Marblestone is CEO of Convergent Research. He’s had a very interesting past life; Research Scientist at Google Deepmind on their neuroscient team; has worked on brain computer interfaces to quantum computing and nanotech to formal mathematics.\n\nWhere we discuss how the brain learns so much from so little, what the AI field can learn from neuroscience, and the answer to Ilya’s question: how does the genome encode abstract reward functions? Turns out, they’re all the same question.\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/adam-marblestone\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/adam-marblestone-ai-is-missing-something-fundamental/id1516093381?i=1000743205259\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/5RD8lxJh0mGSlpEWWExQNG?si=srfZ9QBgRFqvOtJGX8EGqg\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n- Gemini 3 Pro recently helped me run an experiment to test multi-agent scaling: basically, if you have a fixed budget of compute, what is the optimal way to split it up across agents? Gemini was my colleague throughout the process — honestly, I couldn’t have investigated this question without it. Try Gemini 3 Pro today https://gemini.google.com\n- Labelbox helps you train agents to do economically-valuable, real-world tasks. Labelbox’s network of subject-matter experts ensures you get hyper-realistic RL environments, and their custom tooling lets you generate the highest-quality training data possible from those environments. Learn more at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise.\n\n𝐅𝐔𝐑𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐑𝐄𝐀𝐃𝐈𝐍𝐆\nIntro to Brain-Like-AGI Safety - Steven Byrnes’s theory of the learning vs steering subsystem; referenced throughout the episode. https://www.lesswrong.com/s/HzcM2dkCq7fwXBej8\nA Brief History of Intelligence - Great book by Max Bennett on connections between neuroscience and AI. https://www.abriefhistoryofintelligence.com/book\nAdam’s blog. https://longitudinal.blog/\nConvergent Research’s blog on essential technologies. https://www.essentialtechnology.blog/\nA Tutorial on Energy-Based Learning by Yann LeCun. http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/publis/pdf/lecun-06.pdf\nWhat Does It Mean to Understand a Neural Network? - Kording & Lillicrap. https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.06374\nE11 Bio and their brain connectomics approach. https://www.e11.bio/\nSam Gershman on what dopamine is doing in the brain. https://gershmanlab.com/pubs/GershmanUchida19.pdf\nGwern’s proposal on training models on the brain’s hidden states. https://gwern.net/aunn-brain\nRelevant episodes:\nIlya Sutskever https://youtu.be/aR20FWCCjAs\nRichard Sutton https://youtu.be/21EYKqUsPfg\nAndrej Karpathy https://youtu.be/lXUZvyajciY\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n0:00:00 – The brain’s secret sauce is the reward functions, not the architecture\n0:22:20 – What the genome actually encodes\n0:42:42 – What kind of RL is the brain doing?\n0:50:31 – Is biological hardware a limitation or an advantage?\n1:03:59 – Why we need to map the human brain\n1:23:28 – What value will automating math have?\n1:38:18 – Architecture of the brain",

      "text": "It would be a mistake to underestimate the amount of data in the average human mind, but it is not just the amount, it is about how it is accessed, and the \"experience\" of the data.       "text": "A more fundamental problem for AI is what Donald Hoffman pointed out. Our sensory system also evolved and the “world” we perceive and all the “objects” in it are not real.       "text": "A brain is a result of what... 3 bllion years of evolution of living organisms. I think we can count the single cell beings in this too. So it should not be a surprise a \"brain\" is wired to do exactly that.\nIn case of humans these feature is extra complex because we dont have to predict just physical events - to the best of our ability - but a myriad of all kind of other events our specific biology,  civilization and society produce.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "AI will end up eating it's own tail. It's too unreliable, making things up convincingly and wasting the users time. It's also mind-numbingly generic. The over hype is making people think the thing is infallible. Basically, it's a flawed product.",

      "id": "Ugw_QGSAWFIKWklYI1p4AaABAg",

      "text": "I believe that drawing attention to these helpful subjects is beneficial to helping society to continue learning and teaching others how to learn about these subjects.",

    {
      "id": "UgxeqqBERroWu1-wwfB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "One aspect that puzzles me about this neuroscience story as an ML engineer: if the cortext has so much more flexibility, rich inputs and \"power\" than the steering system, how does it not overfit / \"game\" the steering system? Especially when they start talking about the cortext \"modelling what reward it's going to get\", feels like that should naturally follow. (I'm only at the 47 min mark but it looks unlikely that they'll address it when they haven't already)",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCrQGIDIjeX_fbrx_dwspGPw",
      "author": "@MPeti02",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l4ApR6kWIIj38M6PYPbpZ_fdPYmYAdpT314_hzkpORgzU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1768780800,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgxeqqBERroWu1-wwfB4AaABAg.ARo7KXCBjQ3ARoqeSVMMQf",
      "parent": "UgxeqqBERroWu1-wwfB4AaABAg",
      "text": "Karl Friston's free energy principle is kinda getting at this. In some sense when when you glance at something typed and you think you read a certain word, but on a longer look realize it was a different word and your mind inserted an expected one that made sense for your context, that would be an error, or free energy. The longer look updates correctly and our context model adjusts to minimize that free energy. \n\nOur minds basically are running a predictive model at all times until our senses fully register.\n\nPossibly another way we overfit is by living our lives in a predictable pattern. Wake up, get ready in a certain order, drive a path, stop for a particular coffee... Minimizing the energy of change by sticking to the predictable model. \n\nE.g. ever driven a certain direction you always travel, but to a new place, and when driving absent mindedly moved to turn at a street you would use to go to work? Overfit... Had to generalize to a new pattern outside of the minds strongest pattern (your drive to work).",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Dear Dawrkesh, \n\nI am writing to you as someone who deeply admires your commitment to journalism and your willingness to question prevailing narratives in the pursuit of truth.\nToday, I urge you to lend your voice to the people of Iran, who are facing widespread violence and repression across much of the country. Ordinary citizens are being met with mass shootings and severe crackdowns simply for demanding their most basic human rights—freedom, dignity, and the right to determine their own future.\nAt this critical moment, the Iranian people need their story to be told honestly and courageously to the world. Your platform has the power to ensure that their voices are heard, particularly by the American public.\nI respectfully encourage you to examine the vision and principles articulated by Prince Reza Pahlavi regarding a transitional government. Many Iranians view him as a unifying and credible figure capable of guiding the country toward a democratic transition and away from nearly five decades of authoritarian rule that has deeply harmed Iran’s society, economy, and historic legacy.\nPlease consider being a voice for the rightful demands of the Iranian people and a source of clarity for those seeking to understand the reality on the ground. History remembers those who chose to speak when silence was easier.\nWith respect and appreciation,",

      "text": "LLMs represent networks of abstractions collected in human language.       "id": "UgwLs7Arz5l_ZWRtzvd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "It has nothing to do with the function of the neurology… brains are optimized for movement, not consciousness… again neurologists already know this stuff but getting whole industries to cross pollinate when especially all these things are bound to academia and the retardation that comes with academic bureaucracy that bases itself on having recognition vs having new and accurate ideas… functional neurology has already figured out most neurological disorders but it’s not even taught in neuro science classes or neuro surgeons know anything about it…. People assume meritocracy drives these industries but it doesn’t… it selects for Pournells law…",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "LLMs are lookup tables: memorizing the answers during training to answer instantly. \n\nTrue intelligence requires Test-Time Compute: the ability to stop, think, simulate, and reason in the moment before outputting an answer.",

      "id": "UgyEoLYljq1I-3R2qXt4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Hmm... how can you know, when you're already fundamentally excluding the plethora of facts you know just because you can't compute it? And you can't compute not because of precision, but because of the bias that is engraved in the 'language' itself (code) /// (a-note: imho, binary language is merely an attempt at understanding the logic of multi-nodal generative representation ('the analogue'). \ni.e. in reality \"the cat is.\" It's the specific information, which is excluded, that's why it lacks the ability to properly predict probability of its state; there's no collapse or 'cargo-shit' alike; flow is in the wave. Counting can only commence after 2 ;) Thus beware - the Dunning-Kruger phenomena. \nBTW, There's no greater reward than that of an idea experiencing its existence. Which could be the very reason why the stupidity is the infinite. \"Free Willy!\" :) You don't try, you receive the signal ~ so... unless the receiver is corrupt...",

      "id": "UgypJhhO4Y_rBugBKS54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Leaning from neuroscience of the human brain, the analogous language model regions of the human brain are the Broca's area (language production) and Wernicke's area (language comprehension).\n\nEven there, it's clear that LLMs work very differently to the human brain, with a single neutral net for both comprehension and production.  It's also clear that LLMs are doing a tiny portion of what the overall human brain does.  No executive function, no prefrontal cortex, no amygdala, no limbic system, no direct neural links between brain regions.\n\nMulti-Agent systems are a superficial construct by comparison.\n\nThe conversation here about the learning subsystem vs steering subsystem was interesting.",

      "author_id": "UCRXDjsKbCk4jvF6yWFjlE5g",

      "text": "Thought it was a little funny that the ads/spomsor-segments lack captions. I was having trouble understanding a couple words in one of the ads, and turned on captions, and thought the video lacked captions. But nope, just the ads lack captions.",

    {
      "id": "UgzbTRpUKmKtSspS54B4AaABAg.ARPiWzUGR-7ARjBMFQb4NI",
      "parent": "UgzbTRpUKmKtSspS54B4AaABAg",
      "text": "If you don't want the YouTube Ask AI to mix your adverts into the main lecture, perhaps this is what you need to do. Normal YouTube channels interrupt a pickleball lesson to sell you a gym bag. The ads on this channel are sometimes more sophisticated than the main event on a channel dedicated to working through the superficially tricky math problems on the Harvard entrance exam. On this channel, you certainly can't trust Google's lowbrow Ask AI to discern the boundaries. \n\nWhat? You interrupted clue for more clue? Does not compute. Does not compute. Does not compute.\n\nI'm only barely joking there. More than once I've had Gemini 3 Pro, under complex-inference, tangle itself into a infinite loop which I finally had to manually interrupt, after already 100 full stanzas of \"show reasoning\",  where the stanza titles began reappearing like little twisty passages in a maze and a maze of twisty little passages and passages that twist within a little maze. \n\nDo not parse Go, do not exit Colossal Cave.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC5khRFNWuwVQmuFRf5z6Zdw",
      "author": "@afterthesmash",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nzf_38osY0eh7aPQbfKu6wRof-DTAs7pSaNm9ZMqGPUJFfWyS5SFzzSHFBOz2qGsV8gw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

    {
      "id": "Ugx1MjGXNDOoVzPjdz54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "It's funny (ironic) that you chose a spider as example. I worked at Spider Pharm where we extracted venom from spiders for research and industry. The fight-or-flight response seems to be a built in function triggered by the visual system. Just looking at a spider drawing can elicit the effects.\n\nOne thing I keep seeing in the field of AI research is mistaking the map for the territory. These are models for a very limited set of examinations. For example, that neural network doesn't actually exist anywhere save the flow chart you're looking at - it's a conceptual model that's simulated through linear algebra. Not only does it not exist, the simulation doesn't even function as described in the logic diagram. \"Reward\" is similarly mistaken - within AI reward is nothing more than a programmed goal, while in biology it's deeply tied into our emotional subsystems. Reward in us triggers something that an AI (running on a digital computer) can never have. Meaning is fundamental to our intelligence, not vector mapping.",
      "like_count": 22,
      "author_id": "UCMcrpoCiclRfW33OMVWSUfQ",
      "author": "@TheDeadlyDan",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nm7FxBHSqYkbNVTfqMKLdKoDrQASQDx04raKNbjQeKzlQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "3 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1768780800,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugx1MjGXNDOoVzPjdz54AaABAg.ARPi8yvcSaTARU9kkjF7qp",
      "parent": "Ugx1MjGXNDOoVzPjdz54AaABAg",
      "text": "It's like applying the engineering method instead of the scientific method.\nWe can't build a digital model without understanding the fundamentals, and we're so far from it. Even the separation between conscious and subconscious calculations are really not well understood, so talking about fine predictors and amygdala is like skipping a few thousand steps.",

      "id": "Ugwfe_HxEb2XKKAkkI54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "A Neuroscience-Aligned Justification for the Unified E.L.A.E.N.A. Core Architecture\nAbstract:\n\n\nRecent advances in neuroscience suggest that biological intelligence arises not from exotic learning architectures, but from the interaction between a general-purpose learning system and evolutionarily encoded reward and steering mechanisms. This document formalizes the Unified E.L.A.E.N.A. Core Architecture as an artificial intelligence system explicitly aligned with these biological principles, while incorporating architectural safeguards that prevent the emergence of autonomous agency. By separating world-model learning from value specification and governance, E.L.A.E.N.A. mirrors the functional decomposition of the human brain without inheriting its evolutionary failure modes.\n1. Intelligence as World-Model Learning, Not Task Optimization\nContemporary neuroscience increasingly supports the view that the cortex functions as a general-purpose predictive system, capable of learning joint probability distributions over sensory, cognitive, and abstract variables. This enables omnidirectional inference—the ability to infer missing variables from any subset of known variables—rather than unidirectional prediction alone.\nIn contrast, most modern AI systems (e.g., large language models) are optimized for narrow conditional prediction tasks, such as next-token prediction. While effective for linguistic competence, such systems lack persistent, causally grounded world models.\nE.L.A.E.N.A. explicitly prioritizes world-model construction over surface-level prediction, implementing causal, abstract, and temporal reasoning modules designed to approximate omnidirectional inference rather than sequence continuation.\n2. Biological Intelligence Separates Learning from Steering\nNeuroscience distinguishes between two functionally distinct subsystems:\n2.1 The Learning Subsystem\nPrimarily cortical\nArchitecturally uniform\nHighly plastic\nResponsible for:\nConcept formation\nAbstraction\nCausal modeling\nGeneralization\n2.2 The Steering Subsystem\nSubcortical and neuromodulatory\nGenetically specified\nComposed of diverse, specialized circuits\nResponsible for:\nReward signaling\nValence assignment\nMotivation and prioritization\nEvolution encodes values and learning pressures, not detailed world knowledge. The learning subsystem acquires a model of the world, which is then coupled to innate reward functions to guide behavior.\nThis division explains how a compact genome can produce flexible, general intelligence.\n3. The Central Insight: Reward Functions Are the True Bottleneck\nBiological intelligence does not arise from superior data efficiency alone, but from rich, structured, evolutionarily accumulated reward functions that impose an implicit learning curriculum on the cortex.\nCurrent AI systems typically employ:\nSimple scalar loss functions\nSparse or post-hoc reinforcement\nWeak or externally imposed alignment\nThis mismatch explains why modern models require orders of magnitude more data to approximate human-like understanding.\n4. E.L.A.E.N.A.’s Architectural Response\nE.L.A.E.N.A. adopts the biological insight without inheriting biological risk by implementing a strict architectural separation:\n4.1 Learning Without Value Ownership\nWorld models are learned\nConcepts are formed\nCausal relationships are inferred\nNo intrinsic goals or drives are instantiated\n4.2 Steering Without Agency\nValue signals exist\nConstraints and priorities exist\nGovernance layers impose directionality\nBut these signals do not generate self-directed optimization\nThis mirrors the biological learning/steering split while preventing the evolutionary coupling that produces survival-driven agency.\n5. Reinforcement Learning Without Autonomous Drives\nBiological brains utilize both:\nModel-free reinforcement learning (habitual value caching)\nModel-based reinforcement learning (planning using world models)\nE.L.A.E.N.A. incorporates evaluation and feedback mechanisms analogous to reinforcement learning without permitting internal reward maximization loops. All evaluative signals are externally governed and architecturally constrained.\nThis prevents:\nReward hacking\nSelf-reinforcing goal formation\nInstrumental convergence\n6. Governance as Architecture, Not Training\nUnlike biological systems—where values emerge from evolutionary history and cannot be revised—E.L.A.E.N.A. encodes governance as a first-class architectural layer.\nKey properties:\nValues are explicit, inspectable, and revisable\nLearning is bounded by verification-before-decode\nCapability expansion is gated by comprehension\nNo self-preservation or goal continuity exists\nThis replaces evolutionary selection with deliberate, human-centered oversight.\n7. Why This Alignment Is Structurally Stable\nThe architecture is stable because:\nIntelligence increases do not increase agency\nImproved world models do not grant authority\nValue signals cannot be reinterpreted as goals\nThere is no internal incentive to bypass constraints\nThis reflects a core lesson from neuroscience:\nLearning systems become dangerous only when learning, value, and action authority collapse into a single loop.\nE.L.A.E.N.A. permanently prevents that collapse.\n8. Conclusion\nThe Unified E.L.A.E.N.A. Core Architecture represents a neuroscience-consistent path toward general intelligence that preserves biological learning strengths while eliminating biological failure modes. By separating world-model learning from value ownership and embedding governance at the architectural level, E.L.A.E.N.A. demonstrates that intelligence does not require agency, and that safety is best achieved not through training alone, but through structural design.",

      "text": "we have 2 brain hemishperes , or how ever you write that word ,\nThe left hemisphere primarily controls language, logic, and analytical tasks, \nwhile the right hemisphere governs creativity, spatial awareness, and artistic skills , emotions.\nwe need 2 AI's to get ONE AGI , one for language , logic , etc \nand one for the other stuff , let them work together and voila ... \nif you now build it a body with pain receptors that shock it's brain in a similar way ,\nyou'll have yourself a working AGI ... \npeople forget we have 2 hemispheres , \nso we're going to need at least 2 , if not more AI's to work together .\nmaybe an AI for each of the aspects of our brain , one for language , one for logic and so on ...\nyou want to bet that This is How we're going to solve the problem ... \nit's going take up an entire country's real estate and a lot of power , \nbut it could be done , if we had more power and land to put it on ... \ni'm sure of it , we ourselves are nothing more then chemical machines , \nall the nonsense around words like ''love'' , are just That , nonsense \nit's all just a chemical reaction , which You ... react to ... \nnothing special and definitely not that intelligent , \nif the junk we made Now , IS already smarter then us , \neven without the extra knowledge of emotion and interaction with reality ,\n''a purpose'' , so to say.\nthat's the part that's missing , the other half of the brain\nthose two halfs work together to create our own consciousness , \nso we're Probably going to need that in a AGI too , don't you think ?",

      "id": "UgybDp_4pcZqT-zuNil4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The brain seems to be really good at creating maps, and it may be one of the keys to generalization. I like to think of it as an abstraction layer above pure association. The concept of \"handle\" may be associated with \"door\" and \"mug\", but there is also a piece of our understanding which knows how to navigate around a mug or a door to find the handle. That navigation piece I think is key. Our current models seem to have an emergent sense of navigation between concepts, but I think there are good results to be found in exploring architectures that explicitly build in this feature. Food for thought",

      "author_id": "UCA3-JyczFm9AbpUnYtTu7hQ",

      "parent": "UgybDp_4pcZqT-zuNil4AaABAg",
      "text": "I agree and I would take it a step further and argue that “who someone is” is mostly stored outside the brain. The same way a bitcoin wallet is not stored inside a house but rather distributed throughout the world. Or how on a minecraft server, if your items are hidden amongst 50 secret chests, the items are not stored in your brain. Your brain simply holds the key, a map to where the items are or the bitcoin key. Without you, the knowledge is completely lost, even though 99.9% of the data is stored outside you. You are just a map.",

      "parent": "UgybDp_4pcZqT-zuNil4AaABAg",
      "text": "Adam discussed one layer of abstraction between PFC and basal ganglia, but there might be several layers of abstraction in the brain.       "id": "UgybKlazcilt4-Ty-bh4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "33:13 as I'm listening to this, I'm thinking about symmetry groups for material science. Symmetry groups are typically mathematically closed groups where by combining different operations you can get unique versions of a operation. It might be the case that there's some level of symmetry groups that can lead to some of the species-specific behaviors, right? You might find that one symmetry group is a version of behaviors that are well-adapted for a prey animal and then one for a predator animal. Some that are better adapted for aquatic and some that are adapted for land.\n\nAnd what you would find is that while some of the operations, the fundamental building blocks or proteins that are specified are unique, you can get to a large number of cell types from a small number of proteins simply combined in different ways. The different possible combinations could be a closed group. A closed group which could simplify the theory or give more insight into how the proteins combine.\n\nI bet that there is such a set of proteins that govern neuron formation and behavior that are not governing other behaviors in other parts of the body but are specific to neurons. Each of these proteins has relatively independent behavior from other genes but not from the neuron behavior or neuron expression genes.\n\nAnd so the total number of neurons that we have instructions for would be the combinatorics of allowed combinations of these different proteins that help construct different neurons. Thus with a small set of genes you can create a closed group of expected neuron behaviors.",

      "text": "The biology of the brain also expends significant energy budget on sustainable and still has enough energy to think. This energy constraints may also be the reason for the single threaded nature of attention/self awareness.",

      "parent": "UgwUiZHrNwvK8PiX8zp4AaABAg",
      "text": "Single threading in the human brain is an aspect of our language subsystems (Wernicke's area and Broca's area), not the entire brain.  Not only is our brain stem coordinating our body, and our hippocampus coordinating our limbic responses, we also have various other thinking modes occurring in parallel, such as:\n- our predictive human world model\n- visual-spatial thinking\n- sense of time, rhythm, pattern and connection\n- abstraction, construction and deconstruction\n- free association\n- our imagination, wonder and humour\n- alerts and risks\n\nWhen you move beyond language, our brain is doing heaps of different things all at the same time, and some of those things are thinking activities without words.",

      "text": " @SuperMemoVideo  idk me, u, randoms. this is all one big community on this rock. divisions are abstractions and abstractions make inefficiencies, not efficiencies. ever abstraction has a cost. that cost is the time and energy to onboard every human who needs to interface with a given component. since components can't actually be trusted without a TPM and dm-verity setup, humans need to be able to verify their own codebases. the average community member needs help and onboarding and a private or public spotlight. every opinion matters to the weights.",

## Description

Adam Marblestone is CEO of Convergent Research. He’s had a very interesting past life; Research Scientist at Google Deepmind on their neuroscient team; has worked on brain computer interfaces to quantum computing and nanotech to formal mathematics.

Where we discuss how the brain learns so much from so little, what the AI field can learn from neuroscience, and the answer to Ilya’s question: how does the genome encode abstract reward functions? Turns out, they’re all the same question.

of investment, do they still need some of those?&nbsp; Do they still have some of those gaps&nbsp; or is it only more neglected fields?&nbsp; We're even finding some interesting&nbsp; ones in actual astronomy, actual&nbsp;&nbsp;

telescopes that have not been explored. Maybe because if you're getting above a&nbsp;&nbsp; critical mass-size project, then you have to&nbsp; have a really big project and that's a more&nbsp;&nbsp; bureaucratic process with the federal agencies.

I guess you just need scale in every single&nbsp;&nbsp; domain of science these days. Yeah, I think you need scale in&nbsp;&nbsp; many of the domains of science. That does not mean that the&nbsp;&nbsp;

low-scale work is not important. It does not mean that creativity,&nbsp;&nbsp; serendipity, etc., and each student pursuing&nbsp; a totally different direction or thesis that&nbsp;&nbsp; you see in universities is not also really key.

But I think some amount of scalable infrastructure&nbsp;&nbsp; is missing in essentially every area&nbsp; of science, even math, which is crazy.&nbsp; Because mathematicians I thought just needed&nbsp; whiteboards, but they actually need Lean.&nbsp;

They actually need verifiable programming&nbsp; languages and stuff. I didn't know that.&nbsp; Cool. Adam, this is super&nbsp; fun. Thanks for coming on.&nbsp; Thank you so much. My pleasure.

Where can people find your stuff?&nbsp; Pleasure. The easiest way&nbsp; now… My adammarblestone.org&nbsp;&nbsp; website is currently down, I guess. But convergentresearch.org can link to&nbsp;&nbsp;

a lot of the stuff we've been doing. And then you have a great blog,&nbsp;&nbsp; Longitudinal Science. Longitudinal Science, yes, on WordPress.&nbsp; Cool.

> Karl Friston's free energy principle is kinda getting at this. In some sense when when you glance at something typed and you think you read a certain word, but on a longer look realize it was a different word and your mind inserted an expected one that made sense for your context, that would be an error, or free energy. The longer look updates correctly and our context model adjusts to minimize that free energy. 
> 
> Our minds basically are running a predictive model at all times until our senses fully register.
> 
> Possibly another way we overfit is by living our lives in a predictable pattern. Wake up, get ready in a certain order, drive a path, stop for a particular coffee... Minimizing the energy of change by sticking to the predictable model. 
> 
> E.g. ever driven a certain direction you always travel, but to a new place, and when driving absent mindedly moved to turn at a street you would use to go to work? Overfit... Had to generalize to a new pattern outside of the minds strongest pattern (your drive to work).

> One thing I keep seeing in the field of AI research is mistaking the map for the territory. These are models for a very limited set of examinations. For example, that neural network doesn't actually exist anywhere save the flow chart you're looking at - it's a conceptual model that's simulated through linear algebra. > A Neuroscience-Aligned Justification for the Unified E.L.A.E.N.A. Core Architecture
> Abstract:
> 
> 
> Recent advances in neuroscience suggest that biological intelligence arises not from exotic learning architectures, but from the interaction between a general-purpose learning system and evolutionarily encoded reward and steering mechanisms. This document formalizes the Unified E.L.A.E.N.A. Core Architecture as an artificial intelligence system explicitly aligned with these biological principles, while incorporating architectural safeguards that prevent the emergence of autonomous agency. By separating world-model learning from value specification and governance, E.L.A.E.N.A. mirrors the functional decomposition of the human brain without inheriting its evolutionary failure modes.
> 1. Intelligence as World-Model Learning, Not Task Optimization
> Contemporary neuroscience increasingly supports the view that the cortex functions as a general-purpose predictive system, capable of learning joint probability distributions over sensory, cognitive, and abstract variables. This enables omnidirectional inference—the ability to infer missing variables from any subset of known variables—rather than unidirectional prediction alone.
> In contrast, most modern AI systems (e.g., large language models) are optimized for narrow conditional prediction tasks, such as next-token prediction. While effective for linguistic competence, such systems lack persistent, causally grounded world models.
> E.L.A.E.N.A. explicitly prioritizes world-model construction over surface-level prediction, implementing causal, abstract, and temporal reasoning modules designed to approximate omnidirectional inference rather than sequence continuation.
> 2. Biological Intelligence Separates Learning from Steering
> Neuroscience distinguishes between two functionally distinct subsystems:
> 2.1 The Learning Subsystem
> Primarily cortical
> Architecturally uniform
> Highly plastic
> Responsible for:
> Concept formation
> Abstraction
> Causal modeling
> Generalization
> 2.2 The Steering Subsystem
> Subcortical and neuromodulatory
> Genetically specified
> Composed of diverse, specialized circuits
> Responsible for:
> Reward signaling
> Valence assignment
> Motivation and prioritization
> Evolution encodes values and learning pressures, not detailed world knowledge. The learning subsystem acquires a model of the world, which is then coupled to innate reward functions to guide behavior.
> This division explains how a compact genome can produce flexible, general intelligence.
> 3. The Central Insight: Reward Functions Are the True Bottleneck
> Biological intelligence does not arise from superior data efficiency alone, but from rich, structured, evolutionarily accumulated reward functions that impose an implicit learning curriculum on the cortex.
> Current AI systems typically employ:
> Simple scalar loss functions
> Sparse or post-hoc reinforcement
> Weak or externally imposed alignment
> This mismatch explains why modern models require orders of magnitude more data to approximate human-like understanding.
> 4. E.L.A.E.N.A.’s Architectural Response
> E.L.A.E.N.A. adopts the biological insight without inheriting biological risk by implementing a strict architectural separation:
> 4.1 Learning Without Value Ownership
> World models are learned
> Concepts are formed
> Causal relationships are inferred
> No intrinsic goals or drives are instantiated
> 4.2 Steering Without Agency
> Value signals exist
> Constraints and priorities exist
> Governance layers impose directionality
> But these signals do not generate self-directed optimization
> This mirrors the biological learning/steering split while preventing the evolutionary coupling that produces survival-driven agency.
> 5. Reinforcement Learning Without Autonomous Drives
> Biological brains utilize both:
> Model-free reinforcement learning (habitual value caching)
> Model-based reinforcement learning (planning using world models)
> E.L.A.E.N.A. incorporates evaluation and feedback mechanisms analogous to reinforcement learning without permitting internal reward maximization loops. All evaluative signals are externally governed and architecturally constrained.
> This prevents:
> Reward hacking
> Self-reinforcing goal formation
> Instrumental convergence
> 6. Governance as Architecture, Not Training
> Unlike biological systems—where values emerge from evolutionary history and cannot be revised—E.L.A.E.N.A. encodes governance as a first-class architectural layer.
> Key properties:
> Values are explicit, inspectable, and revisable
> Learning is bounded by verification-before-decode
> Capability expansion is gated by comprehension
> No self-preservation or goal continuity exists
> This replaces evolutionary selection with deliberate, human-centered oversight.
> 7. Why This Alignment Is Structurally Stable
> The architecture is stable because:
> Intelligence increases do not increase agency
> Improved world models do not grant authority
> Value signals cannot be reinterpreted as goals
> There is no internal incentive to bypass constraints
> This reflects a core lesson from neuroscience:
> Learning systems become dangerous only when learning, value, and action authority collapse into a single loop.
> E.L.A.E.N.A. permanently prevents that collapse.
> 8. Conclusion
> The Unified E.L.A.E.N.A. Core Architecture represents a neuroscience-consistent path toward general intelligence that preserves biological learning strengths while eliminating biological failure modes. By separating world-model learning from value ownership and embedding governance at the architectural level, E.L.A.E.N.A. demonstrates that intelligence does not require agency, and that safety is best achieved not through training alone, but through structural design.
